claims.text: Resistance to time-dependent plastic deformation in high-entropy-alloy multilayer coatings is primarily governed by stable, chemically disordered interfaces.
Chemically disordered interfaces impede dislocation motion.
Impeded dislocation motion reduces creep-strain accumulation under sustained stress.
The proposed coating consists of alternating high-entropy-alloy layers with sharp interfaces.
The fabrication conditions preserve high configurational disorder in the coating.
Chemically disordered, stable interfaces act as barriers to dislocation propagation.
High configurational entropy stabilizes the layered microstructure.
High configurational entropy suppresses interfacial diffusion.
High configurational entropy suppresses grain-boundary sliding.
Stable multilayer interfaces hinder dislocation glide and block creep-deformation mechanisms.
A multilayer coating will accumulate creep strain more slowly than a homogeneous high-entropy-alloy coating under identical conditions.
The multilayer coating will exhibit significantly less creep-strain accumulation than the homogeneous control.
Dislocation motion across interfaces will be lower in the multilayer coating than in the homogeneous control.
The proposed mechanism applies at temperatures and stresses that do not cause extensive interdiffusion or phase transformations.
The mechanism becomes less effective at sufficiently high temperature or stress when interfaces degrade.
